newpost_v0_aswritten: Benchmarking five Node.js WebSocket servers. I compared five ways to run WebSockets on Node.js: default Socket.io, Socket.io with Connection State Recovery, uWebSockets.js, AnyCable OSS, and AnyCable Pro. In this post, I share how a banned laptop, a lying load generator, and a stubborn throughput gap taught me that the hardest part of benchmarking is getting your own measuring rig out of the frame. Here's the result up front. Across the five Node.js WebSocket stacks I tested, raw latency is a wash, all within a few milliseconds of each other at 10K subscribers. They split under pressure. AnyCable held 100% message delivery through simulated network drops, rode out deploy-time reconnect storms with no restart, and led broadcast throughput at scale. Default Socket.io lost about 15% of messages under those same drops and topped out near 120K connections on one box. uWebSockets.js stayed the leanest per connection but needed seconds to recover from a reconnect storm. The full scoreboard is further down. Getting to numbers I'd stand behind, though, started with a laptop and five burned IP addresses. A tour of the Americas, sponsored by an abuse-detection system. AnyCable is our own open source real-time server, so yes, we had a horse in this race, which is exactly why I tried so hard to catch it lying. All five deployed on identical Railway hardware, 32 vCPU and 32 GB, same region, same project. The plan was simple: open ten thousand WebSocket connections to each server, drop them, broadcast through them, measure what survives. The load came from my laptop. It worked for a while. Then it stopped working, because opening ten thousand WebSocket connections to a host from a single residential IP looks, to any edge protection worth paying for, exactly like the thing that edge protection exists to stop. Railway's edge took one look at my apartment and decided I was a botnet. Fair. What I had not budgeted for: the block landed on my whole IP, not just the project I was hammering. Everything of ours that lives on Railway went dark with it.
newpost_v1_substance: Benchmarking five Node.js WebSocket servers: a methodology you can trust. This is a benchmark study of five ways to run WebSockets on Node.js: default Socket.io, Socket.io with Connection State Recovery, uWebSockets.js, AnyCable OSS, and AnyCable Pro. You will learn what we measured, how we kept the measurements honest, and what the results were. What we measured. A WebSocket is a network connection that stays open so that a server and a client can exchange messages at any time; a real-time server must hold many such connections at once. We tested four properties under load at 10,000 subscribers: message delivery through simulated network drops, recovery from reconnect storms after a deploy, broadcast throughput at scale, and the maximum number of connections a single 32 vCPU, 32 GB machine can hold. All five servers ran on identical hardware in the same region. Results. Raw latency was a wash, all five within a few milliseconds of each other. They split under pressure. AnyCable held 100% message delivery through drops, survived reconnect storms with no restart, and led broadcast throughput at scale. Default Socket.io lost about 15% of messages under the same drops and topped out near 120,000 connections per box. uWebSockets.js was the leanest per connection but took seconds to recover from a reconnect storm. The central lesson, and the reason these numbers can be trusted, is a measurement principle: the thing being measured must be kept separate from the thing measuring it. The WebSocket server is the subject; the load generator is a separate tool. When both run in the same process, every delay inside the load generator is recorded as if it were the server's latency. We learned this the hard way. An early result showed AnyCable's p99 latency at 234 milliseconds, but that number was produced by a single saturated Node.js event loop deserializing thousands of messages in sequence, not by the server. A second, independent measurement that timed only the server's broadcast path inside the network put the real figure under 11 milliseconds p99. Two methods, two directions, the same answer.
